newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Blair moves to counter "lie machine".
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair moves to counter "lie machine".

text.p: British Labour leader Tony Blair ordered his party to crank up its campaign on Thursday amid signs that sustained attacks by the ruling Conservatives on his manifesto for the May 1 election were starting to bear fruit.

As Prime Minister John Major kept up criticism of Labour for what he sees as a series of gaffes over tax, privatisation and union rights, Blair ordered Labour's 10-point "Contract with the British people" to be delivered to every home in the country.
"The Tory Lie Machine is now moving up a gear, so it is vital that we move up a gear in our positive campaigning. The contract is the key to that," he told a news conference.

At half-way stage in the six-week campaign, Major believes he has finally got Blair on the run by exposing what he sees as inconsistencies in the Labour programme stemming from the main opposition party's desire to be all things to all men.
The target of Major's attack on Thursday was Labour's plan to get 250,000 young unemployed people off welfare and into work by offering employers a 60 pound ($98) a week subsidy.
Major said the plan simply would not work because it would displace existing employees.
"The truth is: Labour would need to have an employment scheme funded by the taxpayer merely to scoop up the young people thrown out of work by their other policies," Major said.
"If you are a young person and you want a job, do not trust Labour," said the prime minister, in visibly good spirits.

He was buoyed by a a MORI poll in Thursday's Times newspaper showing the ruling party just 15 points adrift of Labour, compared with 27 points last week. The survey gave the ruling party 34 percent support against 49 percent for Labour.

Political analyst Michael Thrasher said the Conservatives had been stuck on an approval rating of around 30 percent for so long that the breakthrough to 34 percent could be critical -- if the improvement was sustained.

"The Conservatives are one of the world's most experienced, most successful political partites. They just don't get (only) 30 percent in a general election, so I've been waiting for this climb-back," he told Sky Television.
But he added that an average of recent surveys by Britain's five main polling organisations still gave Labour a big lead of 20 points. "That's still a Labour landslide," he said.

Blair, stung by criticism that he was ducking and weaving to avoid upsetting key groups of voters, said he would not allow himself to be bullied if Labour was returned to office for the first time since 1979.
He said he would be as tough as any past prime minister, including Major's predecessor, Margaret Thatcher.
"Nobody, no interest group, no pressure group, no trade union, no vested interest of any kind is going to stand in the way of me giving the British people the deal I have promised.
"I will certainly confront anybody who stands in the way of me delivering the best for Britain because if I am elected then that is what I have been elected to do," he told BBC radio.
